name: Chicken Alfredo Lasagna
writer_notes: Source is masonfit.com Chicken Alfredo Lasagna, a small-pan recipe scaled here to 14 servings; all quantities came from the locked skeleton view, none computed by the writer.

REPAIR 2026-08-28 (B2, phantom black pepper): step 2 seasons with salt and black pepper, but the intake had collapsed both into a single Salt line's buy string, so black pepper was used-but-not-bought (audit-spec-contradictions PHANTOM). Split into a Salt line (9 g, about 1 1/2 tsp) and a Black Pepper line (2 g, about 3/4 tsp, bid black-pepper), mirroring the blackened-chicken Salt/Black Pepper pattern. Gram split per the auditor's prescription (3/4 tsp pepper), not writer-computed. Every ingredient is now used by a step and every step ingredient is bought.
Signature swap for this dish: cottage cheese blended into alfredo replaces the traditional ricotta/bechamel layer. Do not describe the cheese layer as ricotta.
Method figures (425F, 30 min covered, 10-15 min uncovered, 5 min rest, 425 preheat) are from the transcription, not macro/cost data.
Prose uses tokens {{cal}}, {{protein}}, ${{cost_ps}} rather than literals per catalog templating rules; no per-line costs anywhere.
No cost_lines were provided in this dispatch, so shop_smart deliberately avoids per-ounce and per-batch package claims and only references the buy quantities shown in the locked view.
FLAG for repair pass: main protein is 'Frozen Lightly Breaded Chicken Breast Bites' - breaded/processed, not plain boneless skinless chicken breast; confirm this satisfies the run's protein gate.
intro_html:
Lasagna usually shows up on the ledger as a splurge night, all that ricotta and heavy cream doing a number on both your macros and your wallet. This one flips the math. We blend cottage cheese straight into the alfredo so you get that same creamy, layered comfort without the ricotta bill, and we lean on breaded chicken breast bites for the muscle. The result lands at {{protein}} grams of protein and {{cal}} calories a serving, which is the kind of number that lets you eat lasagna on a Tuesday and still call it meal prep.

Here is the honest part. This is not a from-scratch, all-afternoon lasagna. It is a smart-shortcut lasagna built to feed you across a whole work week for pocket change. You lean on a jar of alfredo and no-boil noodles to skip the fussy steps, and you put the savings and the effort where they actually show up, which is the protein and the price per serving.

Parmesan Cheese (Great Value): 2 1/3 cups freshly grated (9 1/3 oz) (265 g)
No-Boil Lasagna Noodles (Barilla Oven-Ready): 21 sheets (about 12 3/4 oz) (364 g)

Batch total: about $34.13 across 14 servings, so roughly $2.44 per bowl. This counts only the amounts this batch actually uses from each package, so it is the cost of the food in the containers, not a register receipt.

True shopping cost: about $47.32 across 14 servings, roughly $3.38 per bowl. What the register trip looks like if your pantry is already stocked. Meat, produce, and packaged items are counted as the whole packages you have to buy, since you cannot grab a partial box, can, or jar. Pantry staples you already own (rice, seasonings, oils, and long-lasting sauces) are counted at only what this batch uses.

Starting with an empty pantry? Add about $0.93 one time. That is the extra cost of buying full containers of every pantry staple in this recipe instead of just the amounts used, which puts a first shopping trip near $48.25. Those containers then feed this batch and many more after it.
cost_closing_html: Here is where it pays off. This whole tray of high-protein alfredo lasagna comes out to ${{cost_ps}} a serving. Fourteen dinners that each clear {{protein}} grams of protein for that price is the kind of deal the takeout menu cannot touch, and you already know exactly what went into it.
shop_smart:
The cottage cheese is the star buy here, and it is doing the job ricotta usually charges double for. You need 4 2/3 cups, so grab the big tub rather than the little cups and you will use it up. Full fat or low fat both work; low fat trims the fat number without hurting the creaminess once it is blended smooth.

For the alfredo you only need 1 3/4 cups, so a single standard jar covers the batch with room to spare. Buy a jar you would actually eat by the spoonful, because it carries a lot of the flavor. The fresh mozzarella runs 1 lb 2 1/2 oz and the parmesan 2 1/3 cups grated. If your store sells parmesan by the wedge and you own a grater, that is the move for freshness, but a tub of the pre-grated works fine and saves you the arm workout.
make_it:
Heat the oven to 425 degrees. Bake or air fry the frozen chicken bites according to their package, then roughly chop them into bite-size pieces once they are cooked through. Set the chicken aside.

Make the sauce in one pass: blend the cottage cheese, the alfredo, and a generous pinch of salt and black pepper together until it is completely smooth. That blend is what replaces the fussy ricotta layer, so do not skip the smooth part.

Now build it. Coat the bottom of your baking dish with a thin layer of the blended sauce so nothing sticks. Lay down noodles, then another layer of sauce, then chopped chicken, a scatter of parsley, mozzarella, and parmesan. Repeat the layers until everything is used, keeping parsley on the first couple of layers only and finishing the top with mozzarella and parmesan. Cover and bake 30 minutes, then uncover and bake another 10 to 15 minutes until the cheese is bubbly and browning at the edges. Garnish with fresh parsley and a little grated parmesan, then let it rest at least 5 minutes before you slice.
portion_html:
Fourteen servings out of one bake, and the fair way to split lasagna is by weight, not by eyeballing squares. Weigh your empty baking dish before you build, then weigh it again full and hot out of the oven. Subtract the dish, divide what is left by 14, and that is your target grams per container. Scoop to the scale, not to the spoon.

Lasagna slices firm up as they cool, so if you let it rest and chill fully before portioning you will get cleaner blocks that stack neatly in your containers. Reheat covered so the noodles stay tender and the cheese comes back to life instead of drying out.
